# Linear Programming {#sec-linear-programming}

The methods of @sec-gradient-methods rely on curvature: a gradient step is sized by it,
a Newton step is computed from it. A linear objective has none. Its gradient is the same
vector $c$ everywhere, so "follow the slope" would run forever, and the only thing that
stops it is a constraint. Linear programs are exactly these problems: a linear objective
and linear constraints. They model allocation, scheduling, transport and blending
problems, and they are among the most widely solved optimization problems in practice
[@dantzig1963linear]. The lack of curvature turns out to make them *easier*, in a
specific geometric way: the answer is always at a corner, and there are finitely many
corners.

## The problem

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Linear program"}
$$
\min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \; c^\top x
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
A_{\text{ub}}\, x \le b_{\text{ub}}, \quad A_{\text{eq}}\, x = b_{\text{eq}}, \quad x \ge 0 .
$$
:::

A maximization becomes a minimization by negating $c$, and a "$\ge$" row becomes "$\le$"
by negating it, so this form covers every linear program. A running example: a workshop
makes two products, earning 3 and 5 per unit, and three machines limit production:
$$
\max\; 3x_1 + 5x_2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad
x_1 \le 4, \quad 2x_2 \le 12, \quad 3x_1 + 2x_2 \le 18, \quad x_1, x_2 \ge 0 .
$$
Each inequality is one machine's available hours.

## Why the optimum sits at a vertex

Each constraint $a_i^\top x \le b_i$ keeps one side of a line (a hyperplane, in $n$
dimensions). The feasible set is the intersection of these half-spaces: a **polyhedron**,
a region with flat faces and straight edges. It is convex, so by @sec-geometry every
local minimum of the (linear, hence convex) objective is global.

The objective's level sets $\{x : c^\top x = \text{const}\}$ are parallel lines.
Minimizing means sliding that line in the direction of $-c$ for as long as it still
touches the feasible set. The last point of contact is a corner, or, if $c$ happens to
be perpendicular to an edge, a whole edge that includes two corners.

::: {.callout-tip title="Theorem — Linear programs are solved at vertices"}
If a linear program has an optimal solution and its feasible set has at least one
vertex (true for any problem with $x \ge 0$), then at least one optimal solution is a
vertex of the feasible set.
:::

*Why.* Take any optimal point $x$ that is not a vertex. Then some direction $d \ne 0$
keeps $x \pm \tau d$ feasible for small $\tau$. If $c^\top d \ne 0$, one of the two signs
would improve the objective, contradicting optimality, so $c^\top d = 0$. Move along $d$
until a new constraint becomes tight. The objective has not changed, the point is still
optimal, and one more constraint is active. Repeat; after at most $n$ moves, $n$
independent constraints are tight, which is the definition of a vertex.

This changes the nature of the problem. Instead of searching a continuum, we only need to
search the vertices, and there are finitely many of them.

## Vertices, algebraically

To search vertices we need to compute them. Add a **slack variable** $s_i \ge 0$ to each
inequality, $a_i^\top x + s_i = b_i$, so that all constraints read $\bar A z = b$,
$z \ge 0$, with $m$ equations in $N$ variables ($z$ collects $x$ and the slacks). A
vertex corresponds to a **basic feasible solution**: choose $m$ of the variables to be
*basic*, set the other $N - m$ (*nonbasic*) to zero, and solve the $m \times m$ system for
the basic ones. If the solution is nonnegative, it is a vertex.

In the workshop example, the origin is the basic solution with the three slacks basic
($s = (4, 12, 18)$, every machine idle) and $x_1 = x_2 = 0$ nonbasic. There are at most
$\binom{N}{m}$ choices of basis, so trying them all would solve any linear program,
but that number grows exponentially. The simplex method visits only a short, improving
sequence of them.

## The simplex method

The simplex method walks from vertex to adjacent vertex (two vertices are adjacent when
their bases differ in one variable, so they are joined by an edge) and never goes
uphill.

::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm — The simplex method (one pivot)"}
At a basic feasible solution with basis matrix $B$ (the columns of $\bar A$ for the basic
variables) and basic costs $c_B$:

1. **Reduced costs.** For each nonbasic variable $j$, compute
   $\bar c_j = c_j - c_B^\top B^{-1} \bar a_j$: the rate at which the objective changes per
   unit of $z_j$ when $z_j$ is increased from zero and the basic variables adjust to keep
   $\bar A z = b$.
2. **Optimality test.** If every $\bar c_j \ge 0$, no edge leads downhill: stop, the
   vertex is optimal.
3. **Entering variable.** Otherwise pick a nonbasic $j$ with $\bar c_j < 0$.
4. **Ratio test.** Moving along the edge, the basic variables change at rates
   $-d$ with $d = B^{-1} \bar a_j$. If $d \le 0$, nothing ever hits zero and the
   objective decreases without bound: stop, **unbounded**. Otherwise the step is
   $\theta = \min_{i : d_i > 0} z_{B,i}/d_i$, and the basic variable that attains the
   minimum is the **leaving variable**: the first constraint that becomes tight.
5. **Pivot.** Swap the entering and leaving variables in the basis. The new basis is an
   adjacent vertex with an objective lower by $\theta\,\lvert \bar c_j \rvert$.
:::

Each pivot is a linear-algebra update on the tableau (the constraint matrix together with
the objective row), so it is cheap. The walk on the workshop problem:

```{python}
#| label: fig-lp-polytope
#| fig-cap: "The workshop problem: the shaded feasible region (one edge per machine constraint plus the two axes) and the sequence of vertices the simplex method visits, each pivot a move along one edge to an adjacent vertex with a better objective, ending at the optimum (star)."
import numpy as np

from optimlab.backends import scipy_linprog
from optimlab.optimizers.linear_programming import LinearProgram, simplex
from optimlab.viz import markdown_table, polytope_figure

# maximize 3x1 + 5x2, written as minimizing its negative
lp = LinearProgram(name="workshop", c=[-3.0, -5.0],
                   A_ub=[[1, 0], [0, 2], [3, 2]], b_ub=[4, 12, 18])
result = simplex(lp)
fig = polytope_figure(lp, result)
fig.update_layout(title="The workshop problem")
fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-simplex-walk
#| tbl-cap: "The vertices visited, in order. Profit (the negated objective) rises at every pivot."
markdown_table(
    ["step", "vertex (x₁, x₂)", "profit 3x₁ + 5x₂"],
    [(k, f"({v[0]:.0f}, {v[1]:.0f})", f"{3 * v[0] + 5 * v[1]:.0f}")
     for k, v in enumerate(result.vertices)],
    align="rrr",
)
```

The optimum makes `{python} f"{result.x[0]:.0f}"` units of the first product and
`{python} f"{result.x[1]:.0f}"` of the second, for a profit of
`{python} f"{-result.objective:.0f}"`. Two of the three machines are fully used there: it
is the corner where their constraint lines cross.

### Choosing the entering variable: Bland's rule

Step 3 leaves a choice. **Dantzig's rule** takes the most negative reduced cost, the
steepest edge per unit of the entering variable. On the workshop problem that is $x_2$
(reduced cost $-5$), and the walk would be $(0,0) \to (0,6) \to (2,6)$: two pivots instead
of three. The walk above instead follows **Bland's rule** [@bland1977new]: among the
candidates for entering and for leaving, always take the one with the smallest index.

The reason is **degeneracy**. When more than $n$ constraints pass through the same
vertex, several bases describe the same point, the ratio test can return $\theta = 0$,
and a pivot changes the basis without moving. With an arbitrary tie-breaking rule, the
method can then cycle through the same bases forever. Bland's rule provably never cycles,
which guarantees termination, at the price of sometimes taking a longer path, as here.
Production solvers use more elaborate pricing rules with their own anti-cycling
safeguards.

### Finding a first vertex: two phases

The walk needs a starting vertex. When every constraint is "$\le$" with a nonnegative
right-hand side, the origin works, with the slacks as the basis. Equality constraints and
"$\ge$" rows have no such obvious start. **Phase 1** solves an auxiliary problem: add an
*artificial* variable to each such row, which makes a starting basis trivial, and minimize
the sum of the artificial variables with the same pivoting rules. If that minimum is
zero, the final basis is a vertex of the original problem, and **phase 2** optimizes the
real objective from there. If it is positive, no point satisfies all the constraints.

### When there is no optimum

A linear program can fail in exactly two ways, and the method detects both:

```{python}
#| label: lp-failures
# x1 + x2 <= 1 and x1 + x2 >= 3 cannot both hold
infeasible = LinearProgram(c=[1.0, 1.0], A_ub=[[1, 1], [-1, -1]], b_ub=[1, -3])
# minimizing -x1 - x2 with only x1 - x2 <= 1: both can grow forever
unbounded = LinearProgram(c=[-1.0, -1.0], A_ub=[[1.0, -1.0]], b_ub=[1.0])
status_infeasible = simplex(infeasible).status
status_unbounded = simplex(unbounded).status
```

- **Infeasible**: no point satisfies all constraints. Phase 1 ends with a positive sum of
  artificials. On $x_1 + x_2 \le 1$, $x_1 + x_2 \ge 3$ the method reports
  "`{python} status_infeasible`".
- **Unbounded**: the objective decreases forever along some edge. The ratio test finds
  no positive $d_i$. Minimizing $-x_1 - x_2$ subject only to $x_1 - x_2 \le 1$, it reports
  "`{python} status_unbounded`".

### How fast is it?

Each pivot costs roughly one update of an $m \times N$ tableau. The number of pivots is
the real question. In practice it is usually small, often a modest multiple of the
number of constraints. In the worst case, though, it is not: Klee and Minty built a
family of slightly squashed cubes on which Dantzig's rule visits all $2^n$ vertices
[@klee1972good]. Problems with a guaranteed polynomial running time call for
interior-point methods, which cut through the inside of the polyhedron instead of walking
its edges; @sec-constraints develops their central idea, the logarithmic barrier.

```{python}
#| label: lp-oracle
oracle = scipy_linprog(lp)
agree = np.allclose(oracle.x, result.x) and np.isclose(oracle.objective, result.objective)
```

As a cross-check, an independent industrial solver (HiGHS, through SciPy) returns
the same vertex and objective on the workshop problem
(agreement: `{python} "yes" if agree else "no"`).

## What these examples cannot show

- **Scale and sparsity.** Real linear programs have thousands to millions of variables
  with sparse constraint matrices. Solvers never form a dense tableau; they factor the
  basis matrix and update the factorization, and they presolve the problem to remove
  redundancy. None of that is visible in two dimensions.
- **Integer variables.** Many allocation problems need whole units. Requiring integer
  solutions turns the problem into an integer program, which is hard in general and is
  solved by branch-and-bound on top of repeated linear programs. This book does not cover
  it.
- **Numerical degeneracy.** Degeneracy and ties are the norm in large structured
  problems, not the exception, and floating-point ties are subtler than exact ones.

## Connections

- **@sec-geometry**: a polyhedron is a convex set and a linear objective is convex, so
  the vertex the simplex method stops at is a global optimum.
- **@sec-constraints** gives every linear program a twin, its dual, whose variables are
  the machines' **shadow prices**: how much more profit one extra hour of each machine
  would earn. It also develops the barrier idea behind interior-point methods.
- **@sec-least-squares** moves from a linear objective to a quadratic one, where the
  optimum usually lies in the interior and the question becomes how sensitive it is to
  noise.
